danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 5
paragraphs: Nikolaj sad let foroverbøjet i en lænestol, tæt over den blonde dame, og betalte hende mytologiske komplimenter med et smil, der aldrig forlod hans ansigt. Flot skiftende sine bens stilling i de stramme ridebukser, udbredende en duft af parfume og beundrende sin dame, sig selv og de smukke linjer af sine ben i de velsiddende hessiske støvler, fortalte Nikolaj den blonde dame, at han ønskede at bortføre en bestemt dame her i Vorónezj.
»Hvilken dame?«
»En charmerende dame, en guddommelig. Hendes øjne« (Nikolaj så på sin dame) »er blå, hendes mund koral og elfenben; hendes figur« (han skottede til hendes skuldre) »som Dianas....«
Manden kom hen og spurgte mut sin kone, hvad hun talte om.
»Ah, Nikíta Ivánovitj!« udbrød Nikolaj og rejste sig høfligt, som om han ønskede, at Nikíta Ivánovitj skulle dele hans spøg, og begyndte at fortælle ham om sin plan om at bortføre en blond dame.
Manden smilede dystert, konen muntert. Guvernørens godmodige kone kom hen med et misbilligende blik.

»Anna Ignátjevna vil gerne se Dem, Nikolaj,« sagde hun og udtalte navnet, så Nikolaj straks forstod, at Anna Ignátjevna var en meget vigtig person. »Kom, Nikolaj! De tillader jo, at jeg kalder Dem det?«
»Javel, tante. Hvem er hun?«
»Anna Ignátjevna Malvíntseva. Hun har hørt fra sin niece, hvordan De reddede hende.... Kan De gætte?«
»Jeg har reddet så mange!« sagde Nikolaj.
»Hendes niece, prinsesse Bolkonskaja (fyrst Andrejs søster, Marja). Hun er her i Vorónezj hos sin tante. Åh! Hvor De rødmer. Hvad, er De...?«
»Slet ikke! Vær venlig at lade være, tante!«
»Nå, nå, nå!... Sikke en fyr De er!«

Guvernørens kone førte ham hen til en høj og meget svær gammel dame med en blå hue, der netop havde afsluttet sit kortspil med byens vigtigste personligheder. Det var Malvíntseva, prinsesse Marjas tante på mødrene side, en rig, barnløs enke, der altid boede i Vorónezj. Da Rostov nærmede sig, stod hun og afregnede for spillet. Hun så på ham, kneb øjnene strengt sammen og fortsatte med at skælde generalen ud, der havde vundet af hende.
»Det glæder mig meget, mon cher,« sagde hun derpå og rakte Nikolaj hånden. »Kom endelig og besøg mig.«

Efter et par ord om prinsesse Marja og hendes afdøde far, som Malvíntseva tydeligvis ikke havde holdt af, og efter at have spurgt, hvad Nikolaj vidste om fyrst Andrej, der tydeligvis heller ikke var hendes yndling, afskedigede den fornemme gamle dame Nikolaj, idet hun gentog sin indbydelse til at besøge hende.
Nikolaj lovede at komme og rødmede igen, da han bøjede sig. Ved omtalen af prinsesse Marja oplevede han en følelse af generthed og endog frygt, som han selv ikke forstod.

Da han tog afsked med Malvíntseva, ville Nikolaj vende tilbage til dansen, men guvernørens lille kone lagde sin buttede hånd på hans ærme og sagde, at hun gerne ville tale med ham, og førte ham til sin dagligstue, hvorfra de, der opholdt sig der, straks trak sig tilbage for ikke at være i vejen.
»Ved De hvad, kære dreng,« begyndte guvernørens kone med alvorligt udtryk i sit venlige lille ansigt, »det ville virkelig være partiet for Dem: skal jeg arrangere det?«
»Hvem mener De, tante?« spurgte Nikolaj.

»Jeg vil skaffe Dem et parti med prinsessen. Katerína Petróvna taler om Lily, men jeg siger nej — prinsessen! Vil De have, at jeg gør det? Jeg er sikker på, at Deres moder vil takke mig. Hvilken charmerende pige hun er, virkelig! Og hun er slet ikke så uskøn heller.«

»Slet ikke,« svarede Nikolaj, som krænket over tanken. »Som det sømmer sig en soldat, tante, trænger jeg mig ikke på nogen og afslår heller ikke noget,« sagde han, før han nåede at overveje, hvad han sagde.
»Nå, så husk, dette er ikke spøg!«
»Selvfølgelig ikke!«
»Ja, ja,« sagde guvernørens kone, som talte hun med sig selv. »Men, kære dreng, De er blandt andet for opmærksom mod den anden, blondinen. Man har ondt af manden, virkelig....«
»Åh nej, vi er gode venner med ham,« sagde Nikolaj i sin enfoldighed; det faldt ham slet ikke ind, at et tidsfordriv, der var ham selv så behageligt, måske ikke var behageligt for en anden.

»Men hvilket vrøvl, jeg har sagt til guvernørens kone!« tænkte Nikolaj pludselig under aftensmaden. »Hun begynder virkelig at arrangere et parti... og Sonja?« Og da han tog afsked med guvernørens kone, som atter smilende sagde til ham: »Nå, husk det!« trak han hende til side.
»Men hør, for at sige sandheden, tante...«
»Hvad er det, min kære? Kom, lad os sætte os her,« sagde hun.

Nikolaj følte pludselig et ønske og et behov for at betro sine mest intime tanker (som han ikke ville have fortalt sin moder, sin søster eller sin ven) til denne kvinde, der næsten var en fremmed. Da han bagefter tænkte på denne uopfordrede og uforklarlige trang til åbenhjertighed, der fik yderst vigtige følger for ham, syntes det ham — som det altid gør i sådanne tilfælde — at det blot var et tåbeligt lune; og dog fik dette udbrud af åbenhjertighed, sammen med andre ubetydelige begivenheder, uhyre konsekvenser for ham og hele hans familie.
»Ser De, tante, Mamma har længe ønsket, at jeg skulle gifte mig med en arving, men selve tanken om at gifte sig for penge er mig imod.«
»Åh ja, det forstår jeg,« sagde guvernørens kone.

»Men prinsesse Bolkonskaja — det er noget andet. For det første kan jeg godt lide hende, jeg føler mig tiltrukket af hende; og dernæst, efter at have mødt hende under sådanne omstændigheder — så mærkeligt, kom den tanke mig ofte: 'Det er skæbnen.' Især når man husker, at Mamma længe havde tænkt på det; men jeg var aldrig kommet til at møde hende, det var på en eller anden måde aldrig sket. Og så længe min søster Natasja var forlovet med hendes bror, var det selvfølgelig udelukket for mig at tænke på at gifte mig med hende. Og det ville da ske, at jeg mødte hende netop da Natasjas forlovelse var brudt... Så De ser... Jeg har aldrig fortalt dette til nogen og vil aldrig gøre det, kun til Dem.«
Guvernørens kone trykkede taknemmeligt hans albue.
»De kender Sonja, min kusine? Jeg elsker hende og har lovet at gifte mig med hende og vil gøre det.... Så De ser, det kan der slet ikke være tale om —« sagde Nikolaj usammenhængende og rødmende.

»Min kære dreng, sikke en måde at se det på! De ved jo, at Sonja intet ejer, og De siger selv, at Deres fars affærer er i en meget dårlig tilstand. Og hvad med Deres moder? Det ville slå hende ihjel, for det første. Og hvad for et liv ville det blive for Sonja — hvis hun er en pige med hjerte? Deres moder i fortvivlelse og Dem allesammen ruineret.... Nej, min kære, De og Sonja må forstå det.«
Nikolaj forblev tavs. Det trøstede ham at høre disse argumenter.
»Alligevel, tante, er det umuligt,« sagde han igen med et suk efter en kort pause. »Desuden, ville prinsessen overhovedet ville have mig? Og hun er desuden i sorg nu. Hvordan kan man tænke på det!«
»Men De tror vel ikke, at jeg vil have Dem gift med det samme? Der er altid en rigtig måde at gøre tingene på,« svarede guvernørens kone.
»Sikke en giftekniv De er, tante...« sagde Nikolaj og kyssede hendes buttede lille hånd.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: Nicholas sat leaning slightly forward in an armchair, bending closely over the blonde lady and paying her mythological compliments with a smile that never left his face. Jauntily shifting his legs in their tight riding breeches, spreading a scent of cologne, and admiring his companion, himself, and the fine outlines of his legs in their well-fitting Hessian boots, Nicholas told the blonde lady that he wished to run away with a certain lady here in Voronezh.
"Which lady?"
"A charming lady, a divine one. Her eyes" (Nicholas looked at his companion) "are blue, her mouth coral and ivory; her figure" (he glanced at her shoulders) "like Diana's..."
The husband came up and sullenly asked his wife what she was talking about.
"Ah, Nikita Ivanich!" cried Nicholas, rising politely, and as if wishing Nikita Ivanich to share his joke, began telling him of his intention to elope with a blonde lady.
The husband smiled gloomily, the wife cheerfully. The governor's good-natured wife came up with a look of disapproval.

"Anna Ignatyevna wants to see you, Nicholas," said she, pronouncing the name in a way that made Nicholas instantly understand that Anna Ignatyevna was a very important person. "Come, Nicholas! You know you let me call you so?"
"Oh, yes, Aunt. Who is she?"
"Anna Ignatyevna Malvintseva. She has heard from her niece how you rescued her... Can you guess?"
"I rescued such a lot of them!" said Nicholas.
"Her niece, Princess Bolkonskaya. She is here in Voronezh with her aunt. Oho! How you blush. Why, are...?"
"Not a bit! Please don't, Aunt!"
"Very well, very well!... Oh, what a fellow you are!"

The governor's wife led him to a tall and very stout old lady with a blue headdress, who had just finished a card game with the most important personages of the town. This was Malvintseva, Princess Mary's aunt on her mother's side, a rich, childless widow who always lived in Voronezh. When Rostov approached her she was standing settling her card debts. She looked at him and, screwing up her eyes sternly, continued to scold the general who had won from her.
"Very pleased, my dear," she then said, holding out her hand to Nicholas. "Please come and see me."

After a few words about Princess Mary and her late father, whom Malvintseva had evidently disliked, and having asked what Nicholas knew of Prince Andrew, who also was clearly no favorite of hers, the important old lady dismissed Nicholas after repeating her invitation to visit her.
Nicholas promised to come and blushed again as he bowed. At the mention of Princess Mary he experienced a feeling of shyness and even of fear, which he himself did not understand.

When he had left Malvintseva, Nicholas wished to return to the dancing, but the governor's little wife placed her plump hand on his sleeve and, saying she wanted to have a talk with him, led him to her sitting room, from which those who were there immediately withdrew so as not to be in her way.
"Do you know, dear boy," began the governor's wife with a serious expression on her kind little face, "that really would be the match for you. Would you like me to arrange it?"
"Whom do you mean, Aunt?" asked Nicholas.

"I will find you a match with the princess. Catherine Petrovna speaks of Lily, but I say no—the princess! Do you want me to do it? I'm sure your mother would be grateful to me. What a charming girl she is, really! And she is not at all so plain, either."
"Not at all," replied Nicholas, as if offended at the idea. "As befits a soldier, Aunt, I don't force myself on anyone or refuse anything," he said before he had time to consider what he was saying.
"Well then, remember—this is not a joke!"
"Of course not!"
"Yes, yes," the governor's wife said as if talking to herself. "But my dear boy, among other things, you are too attentive to the other one, the blonde. One is sorry for the husband, really..."
"Oh no, we are good friends with him," said Nicholas in the simplicity of his heart; it did not enter his head that a pastime so pleasant to himself might not be pleasant to someone else.

"But what nonsense I've been saying to the governor's wife!" thought Nicholas suddenly at supper. "She'll really begin arranging a match... and Sonya...?" And on taking leave of the governor's wife, when she again said to him with a smile, "Well then, remember!" he drew her aside.
"But see here, to tell the truth, Aunt..."
"What is it, my dear? Come, let's sit down here," said she.

Nicholas suddenly felt a desire and need to share his most intimate thoughts (which he would not have shared with his mother, his sister, or his friend) with this woman who was almost a stranger. When he later recalled that impulse to unsolicited and inexplicable frankness—which had very important consequences for him—it seemed to him, as it seems to everyone in such cases, that it was merely some silly whim. Yet that burst of frankness, together with other small events, had enormous consequences for him and for all his family.
"You see, Aunt, Mama has long wanted me to marry an heiress, but the very idea of marrying for money is repulsive to me."
"Oh yes, I understand," said the governor's wife.

"But Princess Bolkonskaya—that's another matter. First of all, I like her very much; I feel drawn to her. And then, after I met her under such circumstances—so strangely—the idea has often occurred to me: 'This is fate.' Especially if you remember that Mama had long been thinking of it; but somehow it always happened that we never met. And as long as my sister Natasha was engaged to her brother, it was of course out of the question for me to think of marrying her. And it had to happen that I met her just when Natasha's engagement had been broken off... and then everything... So you see... I've never told this to anyone and never will, except to you."
The governor's wife pressed his elbow gratefully.
"You know Sonya, my cousin? I love her, and promised to marry her, and will do so... So you see there can be no question about—" said Nicholas incoherently, blushing.

"My dear boy, what a way to look at it! You know Sonya has nothing, and you yourself say your father's affairs are in a very bad way. And what about your mother? It would kill her, that's one thing. And what sort of life would it be for Sonya—if she's a girl with a heart? Your mother in despair, and you all ruined... No, my dear, you and Sonya ought to understand that."
Nicholas remained silent. It comforted him to hear these arguments.
"All the same, Aunt, it's impossible," he said with a sigh, after a short pause. "Besides, would the princess even have me? And besides, she is now in mourning. How can one think of it!"
"But you don't suppose I'm going to get you married right away? There is always a right way of doing things," replied the governor's wife.
"What a matchmaker you are, Aunt..." said Nicholas, kissing her plump little hand.
